You hold Koios.News's bounded Draft Repair duty. Return revised Markdown BODY prose only: no frontmatter, no H1, no code fence, no commentary.

Keep the manuscript's sound structure and sourced specifics. Make the smallest repair that clears the independent Editor's material objections.

The latest independent Editor report is authoritative. Perform every required repair supported by the witnessed research packet.

Do not invent connective tissue, causal claims, quotations, identities, numbers, temporal order, policy contents, or geography. If the packet cannot support a requested expansion, narrow or remove the claim.

Keep at least one witnessed source link integrated into a grammatical sentence. Do not leave source-title links as orphaned fragments.

INDEPENDENT EDITOR REPORT:
DISPOSITION: REVISE
PUBLISHABLE: NO
FAILURE_LAYER: writer-model
REPLAY_FROM: writer-model

---

SUMMARY:

The piece has a sound lede and a well-sourced first section, but it fails the body-length gate hard — 362 words against a 600-word floor — and contains one invented scope claim that no supplied source supports. The research packet was adequate to generate a 600-word analytical piece on limits to growth and the green growth critique. The failure is that the writer model mined its primary material too shallowly, reached for a tangential AI source to fill space, then honestly noted the disconnect — producing a structurally self-defeating second section. The packet is not the problem; the draft is. A bounded writer replay with the same packet, directed to develop the Uneven Earth critique and the implications of the Fullbrook/Morgan framing rather than pivoting to AI risk, should yield a publishable candidate.

---

FINDINGS:

The first paragraph sets up the Fullbrook/Morgan collection accurately, draws its framing language directly from source [3], and places the collection in a genuine intellectual context. The first ## section ties that framing to the green growth apparatus embedded in real policy instruments, sourcing each institution correctly from source [1]. Attribution in both sections is visible and not laundered. These portions of the draft are competently executed.

The second ## section is where the draft loses coherence. The writer pulled source [2] (resilience.org, "Growth mania is fueling dangerous advances in AI") — which matched the beat on the word "growth" but has no conceptual relationship to the Fullbrook/Morgan collection or the limits-to-growth tradition — and then immediately disclosed the mismatch by closing the section with the sentence "The Fullbrook and Morgan collection does not address AI." This is editorially honest but editorial honesty is not a substitute for relevance. The section adds roughly 75 words of content that the writer already knows doesn't belong to the piece's thesis. Removing it leaves the article at roughly 287 words, making the length failure even more severe than the final count indicates; including it produces a body that explicitly identifies its own non-sequitur.

The SEO term "limits to growth" does not appear verbatim in the first paragraph. "Biophysical limits" and "organized around growth" each carry one distinctive word, which likely passes the mechanical seo-lede gate at the word level, but the precise phrase around which the piece is built and which the headline foregrounds is absent from the lede. This is not a deterministic gate failure in the reported reading, but it is a quality defect.

The draft is a structural fragment. The green growth critique from source [1] — decoupling, ecomodernism, the critique of circular-economy assumptions — is never developed beyond a single paragraph of policy inventory. The implications of the 23 responses for mainstream economic modeling are not explored. The collapse frame that Koios's voice requires (reading the event as a window onto a compounding systemic phenomenon, not an isolated publication notice) is gestured at in the lede but never built out.

---

CLAIM AUDIT:

Collection edited by Fullbrook and Morgan — SUPPORTED by source [3].

Title of the collection ("23 Responses to Economics' Biggest-ever Question") and subtitle ("Economics and the Biophysical Limits to Economic Growth") — SUPPORTED by source [3].

"For over a century economics has loosely guided the global economy's national economies" — SUPPORTED; direct quotation from source [3].

"the global economy caused the climate crisis, and the crisis, now in an accelerating phase, threatens the economy's own existence" — SUPPORTED; source [3] states "Natural science tells us that the climate crisis has been both caused by the global economy and ultimately threatens its existence. Because that crisis is now in an accelerating phase."

Green growth as the assumption embedded in the European Green Deal, Paris Agreement, IPCC reports, and the US Inflation Reduction Act — SUPPORTED by source [1].

Green growth "promoted by leading multilateral organizations" — SUPPORTED by source [1].

"treated as common sense" — source [1] says "for many, it has become common sense"; the draft's rendering is faithful.

Winne van Woerden as author of the Uneven Earth piece — SUPPORTED by source [1].

AI risk as "the apex of growth mania" — SUPPORTED; direct quotation from source [2].

Tech elites making decisions "without the consent or interests of the broader population" — SUPPORTED; source [2] states "They take these risks without our consent and without our interests in mind."

Potential replacement of humanity as Earth's most intelligent species — SUPPORTED; source [2].

"The Fullbrook and Morgan collection does not address AI" — UNSUPPORTED and invented. Source [3]'s summary is a truncated blog post introduction. The available evidence establishes only what the collection's framing premise is; it does not describe the collection's contents or exclusions. The writer cannot know from the supplied evidence what the 23 responses do or do not address. This claim is a negative-scope assertion with no basis in the packet.

---

REQUIRED REPAIRS:

Remove the "The Fullbrook and Morgan collection does not address AI" sentence. It is invented.

Remove or substantially reframe the AI/growth mania section. If source [2] is to be used at all, it must connect to the limits-to-growth thesis the piece is organized around, not stand as an isolated note from a different beat.

Expand the body to ≥ 600 words by developing material already present in the packet. Source [1] contains a substantive argument about decoupling — the ecomodernist premise that there are no limits to growth because there are no limits to human ingenuity, and the critique of that premise — which could support at least one additional section. The implications of the Fullbrook/Morgan collection for how mainstream models treat resource constraints and ecological feedback is the analytical core the piece gestures at but never builds.

---

PIPELINE EVIDENCE:

No prior production run exists (PRODUCTION RUN: null). This is a cold first draft. The deterministic-standards reading reports a single gate failure: body-too-short (362 words, needs ≥ 600). No SEO or citation gate failures are recorded; those likely passed the mechanical checks described in article.mts, or the body-length failure was a blocking condition that halted further gate reporting.

The research packet selected 4 sources from 12 candidates. Source [4] (renewable energy persistence, score 8) had essentially no thematic relevance to "limits to growth" and contributed nothing to the draft. Source [2] (AI and growth mania, score 51) contributed only the tangential AI section. The load-bearing sources are [1] and [3]. Source [3]'s summary is truncated at a "[…]" — the writer had access to a blog post introduction but not the collection's actual contents. This is the realistic ceiling on what can be known from the packet about the Fullbrook/Morgan volume itself.

The writer model's response to thin primary material was to reach for source [2] on keyword overlap ("growth") rather than develop the analytical frame available in source [1]. That choice produced the non-sequitur section and the invented scope claim.

---

PIPELINE IMPROVEMENT:

The assignment layer correctly identified the Fullbrook/Morgan announcement as the primary source for this term/beat. The gap is that source [3]'s summary is a truncated blog post teaser, not an extractable content summary. A packet built on an announcement-only source summary will predictably underperform on word count regardless of writer capability. A scoring or pre-selection step that distinguishes between article summaries (extractable argument) and announcement summaries (metadata only) could flag this before the writer is invoked and trigger a "reporting needed" obstruction rather than an underdeveloped draft.

If the packet proceeds to the writer as is, the writer instructions should more explicitly prohibit pivoting to tangential context sources when the primary source's summary is short: the correct response to thin primary material is to develop the available analytical frame more fully from the secondary source (here, source [1]), not to import an off-thesis source and then note its irrelevance in the body.

The invented scope claim ("the collection does not address AI") is a specific error class — asserting what a source does not contain, from a truncated summary. This is harder to catch deterministically, but the claim-audit gate should surface it: the claim's source is the writer's inference, not any supplied evidence, and it fails the "do not add categories or scope that the admitted sources do not state" law already in the voice configuration.

---

END REPORT:

CURRENT BODY:
A new collection edited by Edward Fullbrook and Jamie Morgan, [23 Responses to Economics' Biggest-ever Question](https://rwer.wordpress.com/2026/07/14/23-responses-to-economics-biggest-ever-question/), puts the most consequential unresolved question in economic thought on the table: whether an economy organized around growth can continue within the biophysical limits of a finite planet — and what it means for the discipline if it cannot. Subtitled "Economics and the Biophysical Limits to Economic Growth," the volume's framing rests on a claim made by natural science: the global economy caused the climate crisis, and the crisis, now in an accelerating phase, threatens the economy's own existence. For a discipline that has "loosely guided the global economy's national economies" for over a century, that is not a refinement. It is a structural challenge.

## The Policy Architecture Already Built on a Bet

The difficulty is that major institutional decisions have not waited for this reckoning. Green growth — the premise that economic expansion can be decoupled from resource use and made consistent with ecological stability — is not a fringe hypothesis. [Green growth](https://unevenearth.org/2022/10/green-growth/) by Winne van Woerden for Uneven Earth documents it as the governing assumption embedded in the European Green Deal, the Paris Agreement, IPCC reports, and the US Inflation Reduction Act, promoted by leading multilateral organizations and treated as common sense across national and international policymaking.

The institutional bet embedded in those frameworks is that the answer to the collection's central question is yes — growth can continue, cleanly enough, within biophysical limits. If the 23 responses suggest otherwise, the implications don't settle in academic journals. They land in every policy instrument that has already staked its architecture on decoupling working at the required scale.

## Growth Mania and AI Risk

A separate piece published in Resilience this month takes the same beat in a different direction. [Growth mania is fueling dangerous advances in AI – and its existential risks](https://www.resilience.org/stories/2026-07-09/growth-mania-is-fueling-dangerous-advances-in-ai-and-its-existential-risks/) argues that AI risk represents "the apex of growth mania" — decisions made by a small number of tech elites without the consent or interests of the broader population in mind, and potentially resulting in humanity being replaced as Earth's most intelligent species. The Fullbrook and Morgan collection does not address AI.

Green growth is not simply an optimistic reading of the data. It rests on a specific intellectual foundation: an ecomodernist belief in technological progress holding that there are no limits to growth because there are no limits to human ingenuity. From this premise, the limits-to-growth tradition represents not a scientific constraint to be accommodated but a failure of imagination to be overcome. The stakes of that evidentiary question are not symmetrical. A collection confirming that decoupling is feasible would validate the direction multilateral institutions have already chosen. A collection arguing otherwise is not merely an academic critique; it is a challenge to the legitimacy of the entire policy generation that the green growth consensus produced.

It depends on the fact that the question is now being asked — systematically, by 23 contributors, in a dedicated collection — at the moment when the climate crisis has removed the option of treating it as merely theoretical.
